claims.claim: As regards legislation, the British Parliament is supreme or sovereign but in India, the power of the Parliament to legislate is limited.

verification.reasoning: The evidence explicitly states that the power of the Indian Parliament to legislate is limited by the provisions of the Constitution, particularly in relation to the State List and the conditions under which it can legislate on matters typically reserved for the states. This supports the claim that while the British Parliament is sovereign, the Indian Parliament's legislative power is constrained.

details.reasoning: The question asks which Article protects the Right to Privacy. Article 21 is the only option that has been interpreted by the Supreme Court to include the Right to Privacy as part of the right to life and personal liberty. The other articles (15, 19, and 29) do not relate to privacy.
details.abstention_reason: The evidence does not settle the answer or exclude every competing option.

option_assessments.reasoning: Article 15 pertains to the prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, and does not relate to the Right to Privacy.

Key Features of the Constitution of India
Before we get acquainted with the main features of the 
Constitution, let us revisit some of the concepts we saw in Grade 6.
LET’S REMEMBER
 
Æ
There are three organs of government — legislature, 
executive and judiciary — and the ‘separation of powers’ 
is essential to their effective working.
 
Æ
The legislature makes the laws. 
 
Æ
The law is implemented by the executive, which is headed 
by the prime minister.
 
Æ
The judiciary ensures that all laws made are in accordance 
with the Constitution. It also decides whether a law has 
been broken and what punishment is necessary.
 
Æ
We have a three-tier system of government — central, 
state and local (Panchayati raj system). 
 
Æ
Some functions and responsibilities are reserved for the 
central government, and others are assigned to the state 
government.
The Constitution addresses these points comprehensively. 
It clearly defines the ro

ted to 
follow the fundamental duties of the Constitution. 
 
Æ
The rich civilizational heritage of India, the freedom struggle 
and good practices from the constitutions of other countries 
served as the building blocks of the Indian Constitution.
 
Æ
Its key features define the social, economic, and political 
structure of the country and its parliamentary form of 
government.
 
Æ
It is a living document that can be improved as per the country’s 
needs.

The Constitution of India is the document that many of the 
important officials of our country pledge to uphold. The 
president takes an oath to preserve, protect, and defend it. The 
prime minister, council of ministers, and judges promise to

responsibilities;

checks and balances amongst the three organs of government 
to ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability;

the rights and duties of the citizens;

an outline of the long-term goals and aspirations of the 
nation.

Directive Principles are goals that the government should try 
to achieve. They reflect the direction they wished the country 
take to make India better for all; for example, everybody in 
the country must have a good standard of living. But if the 
government does not make efforts to follow this, one cannot 
go to a judge and complain about it. The DPSP are more like 
guidelines than strict rules. Fundamental Rights, on the other 
hand are promises that must be kept. If someone treats you 
unfairly because of who you are, you can actually go to court 
and the judge can help you.
The people who wrote our Constitution created this system on 
purpose. They wanted some rights that could be demanded 
immediately (Fundamental Rights) and some bigger goals 
(Directive Principles) that might take time to achieve as our 
country progressed.

To answer these and many other questions, a Constituent 
Assembly was formed in 1946, initially with 389 members (later 
reduced to 299 after the Partition of India), of which 15 were 
women. These members represented India’s diverse regions, 
professions, and social groups.
How was our Constitution developed? 
The Indian Constitution was developed and written by the 
Constituent Assembly over a period of almost three years. It was 
formed on 9 December 1946, with its members elected by the 
legislative assemblies of the provinces (whose members had 
been, in turn, elected by the people). Dr. Rajendra Prasad was 
the Chairman of the Constituent Assembly. The drafting work 
was completed and adopted as the Constitution of India on 
26 November 1949. This resulting document came into effect on 
26 January 1950, which is why we celebrate this day annually as 
Republic Day.

10 – The Constitution of India — An Introduction
The Constitution of India is the document that many of the 
important officials of our country pledge to uphold. The 
president takes an oath to preserve, protect, and defend it. The 
prime minister, council of ministers, and judges promise to 
follow its provisions.
What Is a Constitution?
A simple answer is that it is a document that spells out a nation’s 
basic principles and laws. It lays out:
 
the framework of the three organs of the government 
(legislature, executive, and judiciary) and their roles and 
responsibilities;
 
checks and balances amongst the three organs of government 
to ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability;
 
the rights and duties of the citizens; 
 
an outline of the long-term goals and aspirations of the 
nation.
Why do we need a constitution?
LET’S EXPLORE 
Imagine that your school has reached the final tournament in 
kabaddi at the state-level. The opponent is a st

tral government, and others are assigned to the state 
government.
The Constitution addresses these points comprehensively. 
It clearly defines the roles, functions, responsibilities, and 
accountability measures for each organ of government. The 
electoral system has been laid down to ensure that every eligible 
citizen of the country is enabled to vote. 
Other core aspects of the Constitution are the Fundamental 
Duties, Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles of State 
Policy. The infographic (Fig. 10.14) provides us with examples 
of a few of the Fundamental Duties and Rights (which are listed 
in full in the beginning of all NCERT textbooks). The Directive 
Principles of State Policy (DPSP, as they are popularly called) 
represent the essence of the social and economic vision that 
the framers of the Constitution had for India. The examples we 
present in the infographic illustrate the principles they wanted 
governance to follow.

been broken and what punishment is necessary.

DON’T MISS OUT
Directive Principles are goals that the government should try 
to achieve. They reflect the direction they wished the country 
take to make India better for all; for example, everybody in 
the country must have a good standard of living. But if the 
government does not make efforts to follow this, one cannot 
go to a judge and complain about it. The DPSP are more like 
guidelines than strict rules. Fundamental Rights, on the other 
hand are promises that must be kept. If someone treats you 
unfairly because of who you are, you can actually go to court 
and the judge can help you.
The people who wrote our Constitution created this system on 
purpose. They wanted some rights that could be demanded 
immediately (Fundamental Rights) and some bigger goals 
(Directive Principles) that might take time to achieve as our 
country progressed.

10 – The Constitution of India — An Introduction
The Constitution of India is the document that many of the 
important officials of our country pledge to uphold. The 
president takes an oath to preserve, protect, and defend it. The 
prime minister, council of ministers, and judges promise to 
follow its provisions.
What Is a Constitution?
A simple answer is that it is a document that spells out a nation’s 
basic principles and laws. It lays out:
 
the framework of the three organs of the government 
(legislature, executive, and judiciary) and their roles and 
responsibilities;
 
checks and balances amongst the three organs of government 
to ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability;
 
the rights and duties of the citizens; 
 
an outline of the long-term goals and aspirations of the 
nation.
Why do we need a constitution?

been broken and what punishment is necessary.

We have a three-tier system of government — central, 
state and local (Panchayati raj system).

Some functions and responsibilities are reserved for the

government.

Assembly was formed in 1946, initially with 389 members (later 
reduced to 299 after the Partition of India), of which 15 were 
women. These members represented India’s diverse regions, 
professions, and social groups.
How was our Constitution developed? 
The Indian Constitution was developed and written by the 
Constituent Assembly over a period of almost three years. It was 
formed on 9 December 1946, with its members elected by the 
legislative assemblies of the provinces (whose members had 
been, in turn, elected by the people). Dr. Rajendra Prasad was 
the Chairman of the Constituent Assembly. The drafting work 
was completed and adopted as the Constitution of India on 
26 November 1949. This resulting document came into effect on 
26 January 1950, which is why we celebrate this day annually as

details.query:
We adopted parliamentary democracy based on the British model, but how does our model differ from that model?
I. As regards legislation, the British Parliament is supreme or sovereign but in India, the power of the Parliament to legislate is limited.
II. In India, matters related to the constitutionality of the Amendment of an Act of the Parliament are referred to the Constitution Bench by the Supreme Court.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.

(A) I only
(B) II only
(C) Both I and II
(D) Neither I nor II
details.answer: Both statements I and II are correct. I states that the British Parliament is supreme or sovereign, while in India, the power of Parliament to legislate is limited by the Constitution, which is the supreme law of the land. This is supported by the fact that Parliament's legislative powers are subject to the provisions of the Constitution [Constitution of India, p. 176]. II mentions that matters related to the constitutionality of the Amendment of an Act of the Parliament are referred to the Constitution Bench by the Supreme Court, which is a process that exists in India to ensure that amendments comply with constitutional provisions. Therefore, both statements accurately reflect the differences between the British and Indian parliamentary systems.

details.query:
'Right to Privacy' is protected under which Article of the Constitution of India?

(A) Article 15
(B) Article 19
(C) Article 21
(D) Article 29
details.answer: The 'Right to Privacy' is protected under Article 21 of the Constitution of India, which guarantees the protection of life and personal liberty. This has been interpreted by the Supreme Court to include the right to privacy as a fundamental right.

Consider the following statements:

II. 'Right to the City' gives every occupant of the city the right to reclaim public spaces and public participation in the city.
III. 'Right to the City' means that the State cannot deny any public service or facility to the unauthorized colonies in the city.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

(A) I only
(B) III only
(C) I and II
(D) II and III
details.answer: Statement I is incorrect as the provided sources do not mention 'Right to the City' as an agreed human right monitored by UN-Habitat. Statement II is correct as it aligns with the concept of public participation and reclaiming public spaces. Statement III is also correct as it implies that unauthorized colonies should not be denied public services, which is a part of the broader understanding of urban rights. Therefore, the correct answer is II and III.

details.answer: Statement II is correct as State Governments have their own Prisoners Release on Parole Rules. details.query:
A legislation which confers on the executive or administrative authority an unguided and uncontrolled discretionary power in the matter of application of law violates which one of the following Articles of the Constitution of India?

(A) Article 14
(B) Article 28
(C) Article 32
(D) Article 44
details.answer: A legislation that grants unguided and uncontrolled discretionary power to the executive or administrative authority in the application of law violates Article 14 of the Constitution of India, which guarantees the right to equality and prohibits discrimination. This implies that laws must be applied equally and without arbitrary discretion, ensuring fairness and justice in their implementation [Constitution of India, p. 103].

details.query:
Which one of the following in Indian polity is an essential feature that indicates that it is federal in character?

(A) The independence of judiciary is safeguarded.
(B) The Union Legislature has elected representatives from constituent units.
(C) The Union Cabinet can have elected representatives from regional parties.
(D) The Fundamental Rights are enforceable by Courts of Law.
details.answer: The independence of judiciary is safeguarded, which is essential for maintaining the federal character of the Indian polity. This ensures that the judiciary can act as a check on the powers of both the central and state governments, thereby upholding the federal structure of governance [NCERT Polity, p. 12].

details.query:
Which one of the following best defines the term 'State'?

(A) A community of persons permanently occupying a definite territory independent of external control and possessing an organized government
(B) A politically organized people of a definite territory and possessing an authority to govern them, maintain law and order, protect their natural rights and safeguard their means of sustenance
(C) A number of persons who have been living in a definite territory for a very long time with their own culture, tradition and government
(D) A society permanently living in a definite territory with a central authority, an executive responsible to the central authority and an independent judiciary
details.answer: The term 'State' is best defined as a community of persons permanently occupying a definite territory independent of external control and possessing an organized government. This definition aligns with the general understanding of a state as it emphasizes the permanence, territoriality, independence, and governance aspects, which are fundamental characteristics of a state.

details.query:
With reference to Indian judiciary, consider the following statements:
I. Any retired judge of the Supreme Court of India can be called back to sit and act as a Supreme Court judge by the Chief Justice of India with prior permission of the President of India.
II. A High Court in India has the power to review its own judgement as the Supreme Court does.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

(A) I only
(B) II only
(C) Both I and II
(D) Neither I nor II
details.answer: Both statements are incorrect. For statement I, the Constitution allows the National Judicial Appointments Commission to request a retired judge to sit and act as a Supreme Court judge with the previous consent of the President, not the Chief Justice of India directly [Constitution of India, p. 91]. For statement II, while High Courts have the power to review their own judgments, the specific comparison to the Supreme Court's power is not supported by the provided sources, which do not explicitly state that the High Court's review power is equivalent to that of the Supreme Court. Therefore, neither statement is correct.

details.query:
With reference to India, consider the following statements:
I. There is only one citizenship and one domicile.
II. A citizen by birth only can become the Head of State.
III. A foreigner once granted the citizenship cannot be deprived of it under any circumstances.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

(A) I only
(B) II only
(C) I and III
(D) II and III
details.answer: Statement I is correct as the Constitution of India provides for only one citizenship for all Indians, and domicile is determined by the territory of India. Statement II is incorrect because the Constitution does not specify that only a citizen by birth can become the Head of State; it allows for other categories of citizens as well. Statement III is incorrect because the Constitution allows Parliament to make provisions regarding the termination of citizenship, meaning a foreigner granted citizenship can be deprived of it under certain circumstances. Therefore, the only correct statement is I, making option (A) the correct choice. [Constitution of India, p. 35-36]

details.query:
Which one of the following factors constitutes the best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy?

(A) A committed judiciary
(B) Centralization of powers
(C) Elected government
(D) Separation of powers
details.answer: The best safeguard of liberty in a liberal democracy is the separation of powers. This principle ensures that the different branches of government (executive, legislative, and judiciary) operate independently and check each other's powers, thereby protecting individual liberties from abuse by any one branch. This is supported by the Constitution of India, which emphasizes the separation of the judiciary from the executive to maintain this balance [Constitution of India, p. 55].

details.query:
Under the Indian Constitution, concentration of wealth violates

(A) the Right to Equality
(B) the Directive Principles of State Policy
(C) the Right to Freedom
(D) the Concept of Welfare
details.answer: The concentration of wealth violates the Directive Principles of State Policy, specifically stating that the operation of the economic system should not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment [Constitution of India, p. 52].

details.query:
What is the position of the Right to Property in India?

(A) Legal right available to citizens only
(B) Legal right available to any person
(C) Fundamental Right available to citizens only
(D) Neither Fundamental Right nor legal right
details.answer: The Right to Property in India is not a Fundamental Right; it is a legal right. According to Article 300A of the Constitution, no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law, indicating that it is a legal right rather than a fundamental one. Therefore, the correct position is that it is neither a Fundamental Right nor a legal right in the traditional sense, as it does not guarantee property rights as fundamental rights do. This aligns with the information provided in the sources.

details.query:
What was the exact constitutional status of India on 26th January, 1950?

(A) A Democratic Republic
(B) A Sovereign Democratic Republic
(C) A Sovereign Secular Democratic Republic
(D) A Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic
details.answer: On 26th January 1950, India was established as a 'Sovereign Democratic Republic'. This is evident from the Preamble of the Constitution, which states that India is a 'SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC' as it was adopted on 26th November 1949 and came into effect on 26th January 1950 [Constitution of India, p. 32]. The terms 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added later through the 42nd Amendment in 1976, which means they were not part of the constitutional status on the date in question [NCERT Polity, p. 17].

details.query:
Constitutional government means

(A) a representative government of a nation with federal structure
(B) a government whose Head enjoys nominal powers
(C) a government whose Head enjoys real powers
(D) a government limited by the terms of the Constitution
details.answer: Constitutional government refers to a government that is limited by the terms of the Constitution. This is evident as the Constitution of India outlines the framework of government, including checks and balances, and defines the roles and responsibilities of various organs of government, ensuring that power is not absolute but constrained by law [NCERT Polity, p. 3].

details.query:
Consider the following statements in respect of Bharat Ratna and Padma Awards:
I. Bharat Ratna and Padma Awards are titles under the Article 18(1) of the Constitution of India.
II. Padma Awards, which were instituted in the year 1954, were suspended only once.
III. The number of Bharat Ratna Awards is restricted to a maximum of five in a particular year.
Which of the above statements are not correct?

(A) I and II only
(B) II and III only
(C) I and III only
(D) I, II and III
details.answer: All three statements are not correct. Statement I is incorrect because Article 18(1) of the Constitution of India specifically prohibits the conferral of titles by the State, except for military or academic distinctions, and does not mention Bharat Ratna or Padma Awards as titles under this article [Constitution of India, p. 40]. Statement II is incorrect as the provided sources do not confirm that Padma Awards were suspended only once. Statement III is also incorrect because the sources do not provide any information regarding the restriction on the number of Bharat Ratna Awards in a particular year.

details.query:
Consider the following statements:
I. Pursuant to the report of H.N. Sanyal Committee, the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 was passed.
II. The Constitution of India empowers the Supreme Court and the High Courts to punish for contempt of themselves.
III. The Constitution of India defines Civil Contempt and Criminal Contempt.
IV. In India, the Parliament is vested with the powers to make laws on Contempt of Court.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

(A) I and II only
(B) I, II and IV
(C) III and IV only
(D) III only
details.answer: The correct statements are I, II, and IV. Statement I is correct as the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 was indeed passed following the recommendations of the H.N. Sanyal Committee. Statement II is correct because the Constitution of India empowers the Supreme Court and High Courts to punish for contempt of themselves, as stated in Article 129. Statement IV is also correct since the Parliament has the authority to make laws regarding contempt of court. However, Statement III is incorrect because the Constitution does not define Civil Contempt and Criminal Contempt; it only provides the framework for contempt laws. Therefore, the correct answer is (B) I, II, and IV.

(A) I only
(B) II only

details.answer: Statement II is correct as Bar Councils have the power to lay down the rules relating to legal education and recognition of law colleges. However, Statement I is incorrect because it does not accurately reflect the recognition of advocates, as corporate lawyers and patent attorneys can also be recognized as advocates under the Advocates Act, 1961. Therefore, the correct answer is (B) II only.

details.query:
Consider the following statements:
I. A bill amending the Constitution requires a prior recommendation of the President of India.
II. When a Constitution Amendment Bill is presented to the President of India, it is obligatory for the President of India to give his/her assent.
III. A Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha by a special majority and there is no provision for joint sitting.
Which of the statements given above are correct?

(A) I and II only
(B) II and III only
(C) I and III only
(D) I, II and III
details.answer: Statement I is correct because a bill amending the Constitution requires prior recommendation of the President of India before it is presented to the Parliament for consideration. Statement II is incorrect because it is not obligatory for the President to give assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill; the President can return the bill for reconsideration. Statement III is correct as a Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha by a special majority, and there is no provision for a joint sitting for such bills. Therefore, the correct statements are I and III only.

details.query:

I. The Constitution of India classifies the ministers into four ranks viz. Cabinet Minister, Minister of State with Independent Charge, Minister of State and Deputy Minister.
II. The total number of ministers in the Union Government, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed 15 percent of the total number of members in the Lok Sabha.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

(A) I only
(B) II only
(C) Both I and II
(D) Neither I nor II
details.answer: Statement I is incorrect because the Constitution of India does not classify ministers into four ranks as mentioned. Statement II is correct as it states that the total number of ministers in the Union Government, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed 15 percent of the total number of members in the Lok Sabha, which is consistent with the provisions for state governments [Constitution of India, p. 104]. Therefore, the correct answer is (B) II only.

details.query:
Which of the following is/are the exclusive power(s) of Lok Sabha?
I. To ratify the declaration of Emergency
II. To pass a motion of no-confidence against the Council of Ministers
III. To impeach the President of India
Select the correct answer using the code given below:

(A) I and II
(B) II only
(C) I and III
(D) III only
details.answer: The exclusive power of the Lok Sabha includes the ability to pass a motion of no-confidence against the Council of Ministers, as this is a power that is not shared with the Rajya Sabha. The other options, such as ratifying the declaration of Emergency and impeaching the President, involve both Houses of Parliament and are not exclusive to the Lok Sabha. Therefore, the correct answer is II only.

(C) III and IV only

details.answer: Statement I is correct as the election of the Deputy Speaker is to be held on a date fixed by the Speaker, as per the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha. Statement III is also correct because the Deputy Speaker has the same powers as the Speaker when presiding over the House, and no appeal lies against his rulings. However, Statement II is incorrect as there is no mandatory provision that the Deputy Speaker must be from either the principal opposition party or the ruling party. Statement IV is also incorrect as the appointment of the Deputy Speaker does not require a motion moved by the Speaker and seconded by the Prime Minister. Therefore, the correct statements are I and III only.

details.query:
If a particular area is brought under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements best reflects the consequence of it?

(A) This would prevent the transfer of land of tribal people to non-tribal people.
(B) This would create a local self-governing body in that area.
(C) This would convert that area into a Union Territory.
(D) The State having such areas would be declared a Special Category State.
details.answer: Bringing an area under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of India primarily aims to protect the rights of tribal people, including preventing the transfer of land from tribal to non-tribal people. This is reflected in the provisions that govern the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes, which are designed to safeguard the interests of these communities [Constitution of India, p. 174].

details.query:
In essence, what does 'Due Process of Law' mean?

(A) The principle of natural justice
(B) The procedure established by law
(C) Fair application of law
(D) Equality before law
details.answer: 'Due Process of Law' essentially refers to the procedure established by law, which is a fundamental principle ensuring that legal proceedings are conducted according to established rules and principles. This is reflected in the Constitution of India, which emphasizes the importance of legal procedures in the administration of justice [Constitution of India, p. 216].

details.query:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I:
In India, prisons are managed by State Governments with their own rules and regulations for the day-to-day administration of prisons.
Statement-II:
In India, prisons are governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 which expressly kept the subject of prisons in the control of Provincial Governments.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

(A) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
(B) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
(C) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
(D) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
details.answer: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct. In India, prisons are indeed managed by State Governments with their own rules and regulations for day-to-day administration, as stated in Statement-I. Additionally, Statement-II is also correct as the Prisons Act, 1894 does keep the subject of prisons under the control of Provincial Governments, which explains the management by State Governments in Statement-I. Therefore, Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I.

details.query:
Consider the following organizations/bodies in India:
I. The National Commission for Backward Classes
II. The National Human Rights Commission
III. The National Law Commission
IV. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
How many of the above are constitutional bodies?

(A) Only one
(B) Only two
(C) Only three
(D) All four
details.answer: Among the organizations listed, only the National Commission for Backward Classes is a constitutional body as it is established under Article 338B of the Constitution of India [Constitution of India, p. 229]. The National Human Rights Commission, National Law Commission, and National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission are not constitutional bodies; they are statutory bodies established by specific laws. Therefore, the answer is only two constitutional bodies: the National Commission for Backward Classes and the National Commission for Scheduled Castes.

details.query:
Consider the following statements:
I. If the election of the President of India is declared void by the Supreme Court of India, all acts done by him/her in the performance of duties of his/her office of President before the date of decision become invalid.
II. Election for the post of the President of India can be postponed on the ground that some Legislative Assemblies have been dissolved and elections are yet to take place.
III. When a Bill is presented to the President of India, the Constitution prescribes time limits within which he/she has to declare his/her assent.
How many of the above statements are correct?

(A) Only one
(B) Only two
(C) All three
(D) None
details.answer: Only the first statement is incorrect. According to the Constitution, if the election of a person as President is declared void by the Supreme Court, acts done by him in the performance of his duties before the decision are not invalidated [Constitution of India, p. 63]. The second statement is also incorrect as there is no provision in the Constitution that allows for the postponement of the Presidential election due to the dissolution of Legislative Assemblies. The third statement is incorrect as well; the Constitution does not prescribe specific time limits for the President to declare assent to a Bill. Therefore, only one statement is correct.

details.query:
With reference to Finance Bill and Money Bill in the Indian Parliament, consider the following statements:
I. When the Lok Sabha transmits Finance Bill to the Rajya Sabha, it can amend or reject the Bill.
II. When the Lok Sabha transmits Money Bill to the Rajya Sabha, it cannot amend or reject the Bill, it can only make recommendations.
III. In the case of disagreement between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, there is no joint sitting for Money Bill, but a joint sitting becomes necessary for Finance Bill.
How many of the above statements are correct?

(A) Only one
(B) Only two
(C) All three
(D) None
details.answer: Statement I is incorrect because the Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject a Finance Bill; it can only make recommendations. Statement II is correct as the Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject a Money Bill, it can only make recommendations. Statement III is also correct; there is no joint sitting for a Money Bill in case of disagreement, but a joint sitting is necessary for a Finance Bill. Therefore, two statements (II and III) are correct.

details.answer: Statement I is correct as the President can declare areas as Scheduled Areas by order [Constitution of India, p. 309]. Statement II is incorrect because the largest administrative unit forming the Scheduled Area is not specified as the District in the provided sources. Statement III is incorrect as the Governor, not the Chief Ministers, is required to submit annual reports to the President regarding the administration of Scheduled Areas [Constitution of India, p. 307]. details.query:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I:
The Supreme Court of India has held in some judgements that the reservation policies made under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India would be limited by Article 335 for maintenance of efficiency of administration.
Statement-II:
Article 335 of the Constitution of India defines the term 'efficiency of administration'.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

(A) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
(B) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
(C) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
(D) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
details.answer: Statement-I is correct as the Supreme Court has indeed held that reservation policies under Article 16(4) are limited by Article 335 for the maintenance of efficiency of administration. However, Statement-II is incorrect because Article 335 does not define the term 'efficiency of administration'; it merely states that the claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes shall be taken into consideration in making appointments to services and posts, but it must be consistent with the maintenance of efficiency of administration [Constitution of India, p. 88].

(B) Only two

details.answer: Statement I is correct as the Constitution of India does impose a duty on the Central Government to protect States from internal disturbances, as outlined in Article 355. Statement II is incorrect; the Constitution does not exempt States from providing legal counsel to a person held for preventive detention. Statement III is also incorrect; the Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2002 allows for confessions made to police to be admissible as evidence under certain conditions. Therefore, only one statement is correct.

details.query:
Consider the following statements in respect of election to the President of India:
I. The members nominated to either House of the Parliament or the Legislative Assemblies of States are also eligible to be included in the Electoral College.
II. Higher the number of elective Assembly seats, higher is the value of vote of each MLA of that State.
III. The value of vote of each MLA of Madhya Pradesh is greater than that of Kerala.
IV. The value of vote of each MLA of Puducherry is higher than that of Arunachal Pradesh because the ratio of total population to total number of elective seats in Puducherry is greater as compared to Arunachal Pradesh.
How many of the above statements are correct?

(A) Only one
(B) Only two
(C) Only three
(D) All four
details.answer: Statement I is incorrect because only the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of the States are eligible to be included in the Electoral College, not the nominated members [Constitution of India, p. 57]. Statement II is correct; the value of the vote of each MLA is determined by the number of elective Assembly seats [Constitution of India, p. 58]. Statement III is correct; the value of vote of each MLA of Madhya Pradesh is indeed greater than that of Kerala due to the population and assembly seat ratio [Constitution of India, p. 58]. Statement IV is incorrect; the value of vote of each MLA of Puducherry is not higher than that of Arunachal Pradesh as the population to seat ratio is different [Constitution of India, p. 58]. Therefore, only two statements (II and III) are correct.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

(A) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
(B) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
(C) Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
(D) Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
details.answer: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct. Statement-I is correct as Constitution Day is celebrated on 26th November every year to promote constitutional values among citizens. Statement-II is also correct because on 26th November, 1949, the Constituent Assembly of India adopted the Constitution, which was prepared by a Drafting Committee chaired by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. Therefore, Statement-II serves as a correct explanation for Statement-I, as the adoption of the Constitution is the reason for the celebration of Constitution Day on that date [Constitution of India, p. 32; NCERT Polity, p. 6].
